package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 7
	p := &x
	fmt.Println(*p)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 3
	p := &x
	*p = 9
	fmt.Println(x)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a := [2]int{1, 2}
	b := a
	p := &a
	b[0] = 9
	p[1] = 8
	fmt.Println(a[0])
	fmt.Println(a[1])
	fmt.Println(b[1])
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 4
	p := &x
	q := &p
	**q = 6
	fmt.Println(x)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 5
	p := &x
	*p++
	fmt.Println(x)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a, b := 1, 2
	p, q := &a, &b
	*p, *q = *q, *p
	fmt.Println(a)
	fmt.Println(b)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x, y := 3, 8
	p := &x
	p = &y
	*p = 1
	fmt.Println(x)
	fmt.Println(y)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 4
	p := &x
	q := p
	*q = 7
	fmt.Println(*p)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 10
	p := &x
	q := &x
	*p = 2
	fmt.Println(*q)
}
What is the zero value of *T?
options: A pointer to a zero T

questions.text: What does *p do when p has type *int?
options: Reads or writes the int at the address in p

questions.text: What does &x return?
options: nil if x is a zero value
A pointer to the variable x

questions.text: What does new(T) return?
options: A non-nil *T to a zero T

questions.text: Why take *T if a function must change a struct for the caller?
options: T is copied; *T points at the same struct

questions.text: When is p == q for two *T values?
options: When they hold the same address, including both nil

Why can you write p.Field when p is *Struct?
options: The pointer stores the fields inside itself
Field is copied onto the stack first
It works only for exported fields

questions.text: Can you take the address of a slice element with &s[i]?
options: Yes. It is the address of that cell in the backing array
No. Slice elements are not addressable
Yes, but only if cap equals len
Only for a make slice, not a literal

questions.text: Why is &m[k] illegal for a map?
options: A map element is not addressable: the table may move
A map value is always a copy of the key
The compiler forbids pointers as map values

questions.text: What is copied in q := p when p has type *T?
options: Only the first field of T
The address. Both point at the same T

questions.text: How does &T{...} differ from new(T)?
options: new cannot be used on structs
&T{...} is nil until you set fields
Both yield *T; the literal can set fields, new is always zero

questions.text: The zero value of var p *int is nil.
new(int) returns nil.
Assigning *p = 1 changes x when p == &x.
Two independent new(int) values compare equal as p == q.
Dereferencing a nil pointer panics.
In safe Go you may write p+1 for a *int.
For a *Struct you may read a field as p.Field.
&m[k] is a valid expression.
&s[i] is valid for a slice.
Passing a T into a function gives that function the same struct, not a copy.
new(T) fills the allocated T with the type’s zero value.
Pointer comparison compares the pointed-to values, not the addresses.
